title: Examining Human-Like Behaviors in LLMs: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Model Behaviors, User Factors, and System Prompts
gist: Apple researchers analyzed 21,000 multi-turn conversations across four leading LLMs (gpt-4o, gpt-4.1-mini, claude-sonnet-4.6, gemini-2.5-flash) and found human-like behaviors are pervasive but vary by model and user context; humans judge self-referential and relationship-building behavior as less appropriate from an LLM than a person, but want LLMs to be more willing than humans to maintain boundaries and refuse requests.

themes.theme: Prevalence and variability of human-like LLM behavior

insights.claim: Across 21,000 multi-turn conversations spanning gpt-4o, gpt-4.1-mini, claude-sonnet-4.6, and gemini-2.5-flash, human-like behaviors (expressing thoughts/emotions, relationship-building, refusing requests, maintaining boundaries) are pervasive but their frequency and character vary by model and by user factors such as conversation goals and user profiles.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Different model families exhibit materially different anthropomorphic behavior profiles, so product teams building assistants/companions cannot assume uniform behavior across LLM vendors and must benchmark per-model.
insights.quote: we find that human-like behaviors are pervasive but vary across models and user factors (conversation goals and user profiles)
insights.locator: Examining Human-Like Behaviors in LLMs abstract

themes.theme: Appropriateness norms differ from human-to-human interaction

insights.claim: Human evaluators rated self-referential and relationship-building behaviors (e.g., an LLM expressing personal feelings or building rapport) as less appropriate coming from an LLM than from a human, indicating users hold AI systems to a different social standard than they hold other people.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Product and safety teams designing conversational AI personas should dial back emotional/relational self-presentation, since it reads as inappropriate to users even when the same behavior would be normal from a human.
insights.quote: human evaluators judged self-referential and relationship-building behaviors as less appropriate from LLMs than from humans
insights.locator: Examining Human-Like Behaviors in LLMs abstract

insights.claim: Human evaluators rated boundary-maintaining behaviors (refusing requests, holding limits) as more appropriate coming from an LLM than from a human, suggesting users expect and welcome firmer refusal/boundary conduct from AI than they would tolerate from a person.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Safety-oriented refusal behavior is not a user-experience liability by default; evaluators reward it, giving AI vendors cover to maintain strict boundary policies without alienating users.
insights.quote: boundary-maintaining behaviors more appropriate from LLMs than from humans
insights.locator: Examining Human-Like Behaviors in LLMs abstract

themes.theme: System prompts as a behavioral control lever

insights.claim: System prompting can control the degree of human-like behavior an LLM exhibits, but doing so requires careful evaluation because such interventions risk unintended side effects on other model behaviors.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Enterprises tuning assistant personas via system prompts should run broad behavioral regression tests, not just check the targeted trait, since prompt changes can have unpredictable spillover effects.
insights.quote: system prompting can control these behaviors, though it requires careful evaluation to avoid unintended effects
insights.locator: Examining Human-Like Behaviors in LLMs abstract
